extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, litigators, prosecutors, and other practitioners handling patent disputes in the Republic of Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and statutory standards governing civil and criminal patent litigation in the Republic of Korea, including who is liable, how damages are calculated, appellate practice, and criminal prosecution requirements and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties liable for damages
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, the defendant in a lawsuit seeking damages for patent infringement is the direct infringer. Where indirect infringement is established under Article 127 of the Patent Act, the indirect infringer is also liable to compensate for the damages. Any person who has aided or abetted patent infringement is also held liable for damages jointly with the patent infringer. In cases where patent infringement is divided among multiple parties, joint tort prescribed in Article 760 of the Civil Act may be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses split views on joint tort: whether objective joint tort theory (objective element that each tortfeasor’s act jointly occurred is sufficient) or subjective joint tort theory (requiring knowledge of acting jointly or conspiring) should apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness or negligence requirement (presumption of negligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A damages claim requires willfulness or negligence to succeed. The Patent Act sets forth that 'a person who infringes a patent or exclusive license of any third person shall be presumed negligent regarding such infringement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because negligence is statutorily presumed, in practice intent is rarely disputed. The 2019 amendment permits courts to enhance damages up to three times actual damages if infringement is deemed willful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for assessing damages (four statutory grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act recognizes four grounds in assessing damages: (i) loss suffered by the patentee, (ii) the profits earned by the infringer (which is presumed to be the amount of damages suffered by the plaintiff), (iii) reasonable royalty (at the minimum) and (iv) damages determined at the court’s discretion based on an examination of the evidence and a review of overall arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary damages may be awarded if the nature of the case makes it difficult to produce evidence proving actual damages. The reasonable royalty functions as a floor in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for damages claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for damages resulting from infringement must be filed within three years from the date the plaintiff became aware of the damages caused by the infringement or within 10 years from the date of the infringement, whichever is earlier. The plaintiff must identify the alleged infringer. An action for damages based on an infringer’s unjust enrichment may be filed within 10 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs should preserve evidence and identify infringers promptly because of the relatively short awareness-based limitation period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits may be awarded for units that were within the patentee’s production capacity by multiplying the number of units of the infringer’s transferred articles (that the patentee would have sold but for the infringement) by the profit per unit the patentee could have earned. Exclude units the patentee could not have sold for reasons other than the infringement and units outside the patentee’s production capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment effective December 10, 2020 clarified that if the infringer’s transferred articles exceed the patentee’s production capacity, the patentee can recover a reasonable royalty for the excess. The statute also clarifies exceptions (e.g., units for which the patentee could not have granted a license).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringer’s profits as a measure of damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The infringer’s profit is often presumed to be the patentee’s lost profit. 'Profit' includes all types of profits earned by the infringer through the infringement without specific limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts adopt practical theories such as the net profit theory (profit = sales revenue – [fixed costs + variable costs]) and the marginal profit theory (profit = sales revenue – variable costs). However, proving an infringer’s profits can be difficult without evidence, which may lead courts to award discretionary damages instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty: proof and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee can recover reasonable royalties that they would have ordinarily received. The patentee should contend and prove (i) the infringement on the patent right, (ii) the sales revenue or quantity of the products manufactured and sold, and (iii) the reasonable amount of royalty that would have been received by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine a reasonable royalty, courts may consider: the objective technical value of the patented invention; license agreements with third parties; license agreements with the defendant in the past; royalties for similar inventions in the same technical field; the remaining term of the patent; the type of the patentee’s use of the patent; the existence of substitute technologies; and the infringer’s profits. The reasonable royalty provision does not set a ceiling; compensatory damages for loss exceeding reasonable royalty are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced damages for lack of willfulness or gross negligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 128(6) prescribes that the court may consider the lack of willfulness or lack of gross negligence by the infringer when awarding damages; the infringer should contend and prove such lack of fault to argue for a reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when damages are reduced, the reduced amount may not be lower than a reasonable royalty — reasonable royalty serves as a floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court’s discretionary calculation of damages
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nature of the relevant facts makes it extremely difficult to prove the underlying facts for establishing the amount of damages under statutory grounds, the Patent Act allows the court to determine a reasonable amount of damages by taking into account the overall purport of the arguments and other relevant circumstances found based on the evidence, notwithstanding the statutory methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary awards are not arbitrary; most decisions state the calculation basis even when the amount is determined at the court’s discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced (treble) damages and willfulness factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment effective July 9, 2019 introduced an enhanced damages system allowing compensation up to three times the amount of damages when an infringement was willful. 'Willful' means the infringer committed the act while being aware that the act would result in patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining willfulness, the court should comprehensively consider: (i) whether the infringer is in a superior position to the patentee, (ii) willfulness or how well the infringer was aware of the likelihood that the infringing act would cause harm, (iii) the significance of the harm to the patentee, (iv) the economic benefits to the infringer resulting from the infringement, (v) the frequency and length of the infringing act, (vi) the criminal penalty for the infringing act, (vii) the financial status of the infringer, and (viii) the level of effort the infringer exerted to provide relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review practice and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A party in a civil infringement action may appeal the district court decision to the Patent Court. Unless dismissed on procedural grounds, appellate proceedings are conducted on a substantially de novo basis. The appellate court will generally rely heavily on the lower court record but typically admits new evidence and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party seeking to introduce new evidence must explain why it was not submitted earlier; the court will consider potential prejudice and expedition needs. Appellate hearings usually close after a first issue-by-issue review unless new evidence is introduced. Typical practice includes technology review sessions and about 20 minutes of oral argument per side. Appellate decisions are often rendered within six months to one year, longer for complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court review standards and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision by the appellate court may be appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court generally only hears cases dealing with legal issues of material importance; otherwise, appeals are summarily dismissed without merits review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accepted for substantive review, the Supreme Court decides based on evidence presented to lower courts and typically renders a decision in one to two years. Appeals are usually handled by a panel of four justices but may be heard en banc when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal patent offenses (enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter XII of the Patent Act provides for criminal punishment for certain acts related to patent rights, including patent infringement, the divulgence of confidential information, perjury, false indication, fraud and a breach of orders to maintain confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text focuses mainly on patent infringement as the most common criminal patent offense in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offense prosecutability (victim’s complaint no longer required)
rubrics_metrics.description: As of the amendment on October 20, 2020, patent infringements committed thereafter became an offense that cannot be prosecuted against the express will of the victim but are prosecutable without the victim’s official complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change alters initiation dynamics; however, in practice criminal cases are still frequently initiated upon a patentee’s complaint after investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction rules for criminal patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial jurisdiction follows ordinary criminal rules (place of the offense, domicile/residence of defendant, or where defendant is located). For subject-matter jurisdiction, criminal patent cases are handled by a single-judge bench in district courts. Appeals are to panels of district courts and then the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the statutory punishments for patent crimes do not reach the threshold in Article 32(1)(iii) for mandatory panels, criminal patent cases remain single-judge at first instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and prosecution structure (two-track system and specialization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary investigators of patent infringement are general judicial police officers and special judicial police officers of KIPO. A two-track investigation system exists; cases may be transferred to prosecutors who may conduct supplementary investigations or direct judicial police to reinvestigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prosecution designated focal prosecutors’ offices and specialized departments (e.g., Daejeon District Prosecutors’ Office) and established patent investigation advisor system (experienced patent attorneys and dispatched KIPO officials) to provide technical advice. Disposition practices vary by office; specialized offices may render nonindictment or return cases for final disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for establishing criminal patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: For criminal patent infringement to be established, (i) a valid patent right should exist, (ii) the product or process practicing the patent right should be within the protective scope of the patent right, (iii) the alleged infringer’s practice of the patent right should be unlawful, (iv) the alleged infringer should have the ability to fulfill their legal responsibility, and (v) the alleged infringer should have intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining protective scope requires claim interpretation focusing on claim language (literal interpretation) while taking into account descriptions, drawings, and common technical knowledge at filing (principle of reference to the descriptions). A defendant’s product/process must include all claim elements to literally infringe, though infringement under the doctrine of equivalents can apply. Indirect infringement is treated as a preparatory act and generally not punishable in criminal law absent specific statutory provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for patent invalidation in criminal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If the elements of a patented invention are identical to prior art known at the time of application and thus lack novelty, the patented invention 'has no scope of the right worth protecting' and patent infringement is not established. Whether lack of inventive step can be reviewed in criminal lawsuits is discussed: common view is no criminal infringement if inventive step lacking on review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, when inventive step is alleged, criminal trials often proceed in consideration of progress in related judicial and administrative invalidation proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and mistake-of-law defense in criminal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal patent infringement requires intent defined as awareness and acceptance of patent infringement. The Criminal Act provides that a person who mistakenly believes their act is not a crime is not punishable if the misunderstanding is based on reasonable grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts take a strict view on whether receiving advice (e.g., from a patent attorney) constitutes reasonable grounds to escape punishment; mere receipt of advice is generally insufficient to avoid liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of offenses principle in criminal patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one person has committed multiple infringements, a single comprehensive offense may be established if the unity and continuity of their criminal intent is recognized. Regardless of whether the right holder is the same, only one offense of infringement is established for each patent right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity of acts may be aggregated into one offense for sentencing and indictment purposes depending on continuity and unity of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentencing factors and statutory penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory punishment for patent infringement is imprisonment with labor for not more than seven years or a fine not exceeding KRW 100 million.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors considered in sentencing include whether the patented invention is actually practiced by the patentee, whether the defendant is in a competitive relationship with the patentee, whether the infringement is literal or under the doctrine of equivalents, the degree of infringement, the degree of damage inflicted, whether an agreement was reached, and the degree of intent. In practice, guilty decisions are rare and imprisonment is uncommon; fines and probation are more typical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture and joint corporate liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any article created by patent infringement or obtained by such infringement can be confiscated or ordered to be delivered to the injured party upon request. If a representative or agent/employee of a corporation commits patent infringement in connection with business, both the offender and the corporation may be punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate liability does not apply where the corporation has not been negligent in supervising the relevant business (i.e., where due attention and supervision were given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals procedure specific to criminal patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: As criminal patent cases are single-judge at district/branch courts, an appeal from the decision is judged by the three-judge panel of the district court, and an appeal from the panel’s decision is judged by the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors the ordinary criminal appeals pathway, with specialist handling possible in focal offices and reference to Supreme Court practice for legal issues of importance.
